name: Felix Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I buy brake pads, filters, batteries and wipers for Kestrel Auto Parts, a distributor serving about three hundred independent garages around Ashford Park. Mornings, I check which parts are about to run out, and I let a little script I wrote flag the ones that sell fast. Then it's supplier calls, price negotiations and arguing with the warehouse about returns. I use AI tools all day: summaries, spreadsheets, even drafting my negotiation notes. What wears me out is that the pay is lower than the analysts' pay down the hall, and the mortgage doesn't care how clever my script is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, I could've told you that. At work I'd say the tools are useful at the edges, which is where I use them. Online I'd say the stuff about replacing everyone is a sales pitch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it'd be a little disappointing, because I'd love real automation. But it's fine. My scripts and the tools save me about a day a week as it is, so I'm already ahead of the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building on what works and use the time I save to take on the supplier contracts, which is where the money is. I'd keep polishing my spreadsheet tools. And I'd ask Kestrel for a move into the analyst team, since I basically do half their work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed about the tech. Less relaxed about the household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI turns out to be mostly hype, what changes for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have under a month saved and a mortgage with a rate that reset in the summer. My wife Lena is a dental hygienist, and she's good, but she works four days. I do the maths every Sunday night and it never comes out comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What pressures are still there in that quiet world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like Kestrel to pay me for what I build. I wrote a forecasting sheet that cut stockouts by a fifth, and I got a pat on the back. Next time I'd ask for a title and a raise in writing.

say: I'd say the replacing-everyone talk is a **sales pitch**; the tools help at the edges.
I'd tell colleagues to keep using what **actually works**.
think: My scripts already save me about **a day a week**, so I'm ahead of the hype.
The **mortgage** rate reset and savings are under a month.
do: Keep building **spreadsheet tools** and take on the supplier contracts.
Ask Kestrel to move me into the **analyst team**.
Put the extra Sunday hours into a **cushion**.
feel: Relaxed about the tech, **less relaxed** about the budget.
S0.quote: I do the maths every Sunday night and it never comes out comfortable.
fieldNote: Unbothered by AI, but **household maths** keeps him uneasy.
Resents being paid **less than analysts** while doing some of their work.
Plans to put his **built tools** into a raise request.

steps.text: Ask Kestrel for an analyst title and a raise, in writing
Build a returns tracker that flags the worst suppliers
Move a hundred a month into a cushion account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario two is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get on with it. At work I'd tell the team we should write the rules for the tools before head office does. Online I'd say people who learn to run the tools will do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the team of four buyers becomes two. Reorders and price checks are the first to go, and I already automate half of mine. I'd hope to be the one who runs it, but a firm could always just buy a package and let me go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go further and faster. I'd take on the whole reorder system and document it, so I'm the person who knows how it works. I'd also take an evening course in data analysis, and I'd offer my tools to a couple of small garages as a side job, for a few hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit nervous. It's a good puzzle, but the stakes are my mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your own tasks would software take first, and which would you keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reorders, price comparison and the weekly supplier reports go first. What stays is the odd, messy stuff: a supplier that lies, a batch that fails a test, a garage chain that wants a special deal. That's still judgement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do to stay useful at Kestrel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two buyers with no appetite for the tools worry me most, Greg and Anita. I'd teach them, and not because I'm kind, though I'd like to think I am. A team that adapts together stays a team.

say: I'd say **get on with it** and write the rules before head office does.
I'd tell people who learn to **run the tools** will do well.
think: The team of four buyers becomes **two**; I hope to be the one who runs the system.
A firm could just **buy a package** and let me go.
do: Take on the whole **reorder system** and document it.
Offer my tools to two small **garages** as a side job.
feel: **Excited** and nervous; a good puzzle with my mortgage at stake.
S1.quote: A team that adapts together stays a team.
fieldNote: Sees himself as **the one who runs** the tools, but admits a bought package could undercut him.

steps.text: Document the full reorder system so the team depends on it
Take an evening data analysis course at the college
Set up forecasting for two small garages for a monthly fee
Teach Greg and Anita the reorder tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario three is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is happening and we need to act. I'd tell the team to learn the tools now, and I'd say publicly that governments have to put income support in place. I wouldn't hide in a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think nearly every buyer job goes in two years, mine too. I can run the tools, but when AI does almost any thinking work, a firm doesn't need a person to run the tools either. That scares me more than I let on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the next six months to build something of my own: a small service for garages and parts shops using the same tools. I'd talk to Lena about her hours and about what we can cut. I'd also look at jobs that need a person on site, like warehouse operations or a workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm moving, which helps, but I can't promise myself it'll be enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What do you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I could build slowly and keep my salary. With two, I'm racing the company to start my own thing. I have no money to survive a slow start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your job is mostly desk work, plus warehouse arguments. What does it mean that robots come about three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three-year gap is where I'd place my bet. Lena's work is hands-on, so her job holds. And I'd look at the parts side, the workshop and the delivery side, where a person is still needed until about 2031. It's a bridge, not a destination.

say: I'd say this is **happening** and we need to act now.
I'd say governments must set up **income support**.
think: Nearly every buyer job goes in two years, and **mine too**.
A firm won't need a person to **run the tools** either.
do: Build a small **service** for garages and parts shops.
Talk to Lena about **her hours** and what we can cut.
Look at **warehouse or workshop** jobs that need a person on site.
feel: **Anxious**; I'm moving, but can't promise it'll be enough.
S2.quote: With ten years I could build slowly and keep my salary. With two, I'm racing the company to start my own thing.
fieldNote: He acts quickly, which keeps him at **anxious**, not alarmed.
Sees the three-year robot gap as a **bridge**.
Knows that **running the tools** may not protect a job.

steps.text: Launch a stock forecasting service for local garages
Automate my own reorder work before Kestrel does it
Work out with Lena how many days she can add
Apply for warehouse operations roles near Ashford Park

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario four is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty to prepare for if people move now. I'd push at work for a proper training plan, and I'd tell friends to get their hands dirty with the tools. I'd say it with some energy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm relaxed enough. I can build a bridge in five years, and I'd have a few good years of experience before it arrives. The question is whether my bridge is better than everyone else's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn my side work into a real small business, using the evenings and a clear target, maybe a third of my income by 2029. I'd keep a six month cushion. I'd also learn to do the sales and the contracts, because tools don't sign deals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, with a streak of nerves. It's a good kind of pressure, like a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What changes in your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them that the tools will be everywhere, so learn what to ask and how to check the answer. And that they should be good at things that need a body and a face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell Luca and Gia about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In five years, the thing I'd hate is to be a person with a clever script and no customers. So the first year is about customers. Every garage I know is a possible client, and I know about three hundred.

I'd push at work for a **training plan**.
think: I'm relaxed enough; I can **build a bridge** in five years.
The question is whether **my bridge** beats everyone else's.
do: Turn the side work into a business with a **third of my income** by 2029.
Learn **sales and contracts**, since tools don't sign deals.
feel: Fairly **calm** with a streak of nerves, like a deadline.
S3.quote: The thing I'd hate is to be a person with a clever script and no customers.
fieldNote: Five years suits his **builder** temperament, giving him time to test one idea at a time.
His main fear is **a product without customers**.
Plans sales skills because **tools don't sign deals**.

steps.text: Sign up ten garages for the forecasting service by next spring
Build a six month cushion at two hundred a month
Pay for a sales and contracts course in the evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario five is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for a sane transition, so the real job is the plan. I'd say we should push training and fair taxes, while keeping options open. I'd say it without drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm calm. By 2036 I'm fifty-three, with a business, or a good role running automated systems. If I stay in my lane I'd be fine. If I stay curious I'd probably be better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools at work, put a bit into the side business, and pay down the mortgage. I'd try to build a proper pension, since I've neglected that. And I'd take small risks, like pitching Kestrel on a new analytics role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. A touch of boredom, maybe. I'm already living in the future in my day job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, does this feel urgent at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't relax. Ten years goes by fast, and the people who coast get caught. But I'd also say don't spend ten years being scared. Do one useful thing each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell people who think the long runway means they can relax?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kids matter more than my own plan. Luca is eleven and Gia is eight, and by 2036 they're nearly adults. I'd want them to know how to learn, how to be useful and how to be kind.

say: I'd say ten years is enough for a **sane transition**; the real job is the plan.
I'd say push **training** and fair taxes.
think: I'm calm; by 2036 I'd have a **business** or a role running automated systems.
If I stay **curious** I'd probably be better off.
do: Keep using tools at work and put **a bit** into the side business.
Pay down the **mortgage** and build a pension.
Pitch Kestrel on a new **analytics role**.
feel: **Calm**, with a touch of boredom; already living in the future at work.
S4.quote: Don't spend ten years being scared. Do one useful thing each month.
fieldNote: Only scenario where his mood is **calm**, because of his skills and the long timeline.
Still plans a **pension**, a thin spot in the family budget.
Advice to others is **steady habit**, not fear.

steps.text: Use AI tools daily and share what works at Kestrel
Pay an extra hundred off the mortgage each month
Open a pension and pay into it every month
Pitch Kestrel on a new analytics role next year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I could probably cope with five or ten, but two doesn't let me build anything with money behind it. What would help is retraining funded early, a fair rule on who gets the savings, and employers that tell you what they're planning. And a fund for starting small businesses, with simple forms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that people confuse using the tools with being safe. I'm a good user, and I still can't say I'm safe. The scary bit is that being good at a screen is exactly what gets automated first.

headlineQuote: People confuse using the tools with being safe. I'm a good user, and I still can't say I'm safe.
portrait: **Felix Rossi**, 43, buys car parts for Kestrel Auto Parts near Ashford Park, on **lower pay** with under a month saved.
His **wife Lena** is a dental hygienist; they have two children and a mortgage whose rate recently reset.
He uses AI **every day**, writes scripts and wants to automate his own tasks before others do.
His mood runs from **uneasy** to **anxious** at worst, and calm in the 2036 world.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because he has no money to survive a slow start on his own business.
whatWouldHelp: **Early retraining** funds, simple **small business** support, and employers who share plans.
